theme: Job confronts the prosperity gospel; God seems far
readingInstruction: Read Job 21:1-23:17. Job answers Zophar and challenges the friends’ theory about the wicked. Eliphaz replies in chapter 22 with a direct accusation, and Job answers in chapter 23 with a longing to find God. Read chapter 23 as a prayer.
settingTheScene: The friends have claimed that the wicked always suffer and the righteous always prosper. Job’s answer in chapter 21 is simple and devastating: look around. In this world, wicked people often grow old, wealthy, and secure, and nothing happens to them. The friends’ theory does not match what we see. This is the point where Job’s book speaks most plainly against any teaching that promises health and wealth to those who follow God faithfully. Then comes a longing, one of the most moving in the book: Job wants to find God.
observation: Job says, “Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power?” (21:7).
He describes their children as secure, their herds as fertile, and their houses as safe (21:8-13).
The wicked say to God, “Depart from us!” and ask, “What is the Almighty, that we should serve him?” (21:14-15).
He says that both rich and poor die and lie down in the dust together (21:23-26).
Eliphaz now accuses him of specific sins: “Is not your evil abundant? There is no end to your iniquities” (22:5). He claims Job has not given water to the weary or bread to the hungry (22:7).
Eliphaz urges, “Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you” (22:21).
Job says, “Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his seat!” (23:3).
“Behold, I go forward, but he is not there, and backward, but I do not perceive him” (23:8).
“But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold” (23:10).
“I have not departed from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food” (23:12).
interpretation:
Chapter 21 is the strongest rebuttal of the idea that faithful living guarantees comfort. Job takes the friends’ favorite claim and demolishes it with evidence. If the wicked always fall, why do so many seem to thrive? His statement is not an invitation to envy. It is an observation about the world as it is, and it agrees with what Psalms 37 and 73 say. Both say that the wicked prosper for a time, and that God’s justice has a different clock.

That matters for how you read the Bible. Proverbs makes general statements about wisdom leading to life. Job reminds you that those are not guarantees. A teaching that says “follow God and you will be healthy and rich” will break the first time it meets a Job. The Bible does not teach that.

Eliphaz’s response is the low point for the friends. He cannot answer Job’s evidence, so he invents charges. Job has never been accused of mistreating the poor, and the narrator has said that he is blameless. But in order to keep his theory, Eliphaz needs Job to be guilty, and so he makes up sins. This is what happens when a doctrine matters more than a person. It starts to lie.

Then Job goes quiet in a new way. In chapter 23 he stops arguing with the friends. He just wants God. “Oh, that I knew where I might find him.” His problem is not exactly that God is angry. It is that God is missing. He looks forward, backward, to the left and right, and he cannot see him. This is the experience of many believers in dark seasons, and it is described here without a trace of blame.

Yet there is trust in the middle of the darkness. “He knows the way that I take.” Job cannot see God, but God can see him. And “when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.” It is not a claim that he deserves it. It is a confidence that God’s testing has a purpose and an end. Alongside that is his devotion to God’s word: he has treasured it more than his food.
connection: Psalm 73, which you will read soon, struggles with the same puzzle of the prosperity of the wicked. Jesus said that God “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). 1 Peter 1:6-7 speaks of faith “tested by fire” being “found to result in praise and glory and honor.” James 5:11 holds up Job’s endurance.
application:
Test any teaching you hear against the book of Job. If it promises that obedience will always bring health and wealth, it is not the teaching of the Bible.

When you cannot find God, pray Job 23:10 and ask him to hold you until you can see him again.

If you are in a season of dryness, treasure his words more than your food. Put your Bible reading first this week, before breakfast.
prayerPrompts: Tell God honestly where you cannot find him.
Ask him to refine you through what you are going through.
Ask him to help you treasure his word above comfort.
